cards.title: Claim the $1/month trial link before the 3-day window closes
cards.summary: Sequence Shopify account creation so the extended promotional trial price is secured before the free trial expires.
cards.use_when: Opening a new Shopify account for a store build and choosing which plan to start on.
steps: Start at Shopify's official site, enter email, click start free trial, create a password and complete signup. Shopify then redirects to a promotional offer (source describes 3 months at $1/month, roughly 96% off).
Activate the discounted plan immediately, or complete the short business setup questions first — the source says they take about 20 seconds and you still land on the dashboard afterward.
If you skipped the offer in the signup flow, the source says it can still be claimed from the lower-left corner of the dashboard, but only before the initial 3-day free trial expires.
Pick the Basic plan for a first store: it covers launching, accepting payments and running a functional store, and you can upgrade later.
Verify the current plan names, trial length and offer terms in your own admin before assuming the promotional pricing still exists.
caveats: Plan names, trial lengths and promotional pricing change; the source's figures are as-described at recording time.
The source explicitly skips promotional pitches — treat the offer as a billing detail, not the point of the build.

cards.title: Know which three Shopify admin areas actually run the store
cards.summary: Reduce admin overwhelm to Products, Online Store and Settings, the three sections that control selling, appearance and configuration.
cards.use_when: Orienting yourself in a new Shopify admin before adding products, designing the storefront or configuring checkout.
steps: Treat the admin as the store's control center: Orders, Products, Customers, Marketing, Discounts, Content, Markets, Analytics all live in one menu.
Prioritize Products — this is where you add and manage the items you sell, including titles, descriptions, images, pricing, inventory and variants.
Then Online Store — where you select and edit themes, build pages and manage navigation and the visual front end.
Then Settings — where payments, shipping, taxes and store-wide configuration live.
The source claims these three areas cover almost everything that matters; use them as the map, not as a reason to ignore Orders, discounts or analytics once you are live.
Also note the source's framing: your store is technically already live at signup but password-protected, so you are optimizing an existing shell rather than starting from zero.
caveats: Admin layout and menu labels change between Shopify releases; verify the current interface rather than hunting for exact labels.

cards.title: Choose a clean, brandable domain instead of an over-thought one
cards.summary: Domain naming criteria that protect trust and ad click-through, plus an AI ideation method to avoid blank-page stalls.
cards.use_when: Selecting the store domain before running ads, email or packaging that will display the URL.
steps: Run a quick ideation pass with a text AI — e.g. "generate 20 brandable domain names for a fitness apparel store" — to produce short variations instead of starting from nothing.

Apply the source's filter: one or two words at most; no hyphens or numbers (buyers mis-type them and forget whether numbers are spelled out); no unusual spellings that force double-checking; brandable rather than generic. The source contrasts generic descriptors unfavorably with names like Gymshark, Allbirds or Glossier.
Remember the impression cost: a myshopify.com URL or a long messy address appearing in an ad, email or packaging can create hesitation before a visitor reads a single product description.
The source frames the goal as clarity, not perfection — easy to spell and easy to pronounce if heard once.
Confirm availability and purchase inside Shopify where possible, so DNS connects automatically.
caveats: Brand examples are the source's illustrations, not verified performance data.
Perfectionism is explicitly called out as the failure mode; do not stall the build searching for an unused, flawless name.

cards.title: Buy the domain inside Shopify vs. connecting an existing third-party domain
cards.summary: Two connection paths with different effort levels, plus the propagation window to plan your launch around.
cards.use_when: Setting up or migrating the store's domain before launch and before printing or advertising the URL.
steps: Fast path (buy new): go to Settings > Domains, click buy new domain, search the name, purchase if available. The source says it connects automatically with no manual DNS configuration.
Migration path (existing domain, e.g. from GoDaddy): go to Settings > Domains > connect existing domain. Copy the DNS records Shopify provides, paste them into the registrar's DNS settings, save.
Expect propagation to take a few hours; status may read as pending during that window. Do not treat pending as failure.
The source flags a trade-off on third-party registrars: lower first-year pricing but often higher renewals. Buying through Shopify is described as the smoother route for beginners.
Confirm the domain shows as connected before publishing, since launching on a broken domain creates immediate trust problems.
caveats: DNS record names and screens differ by registrar and Shopify release; verify against the current Shopify domain instructions.
The source's preference for buying through Shopify is a simplicity recommendation, not a cost guarantee.

cards.title: Pick and publish a lightweight free Shopify theme before customizing
cards.summary: Theme selection criteria and the preview-then-publish habit that prevents installing a look you have not seen.
cards.use_when: Choosing the storefront theme (fashion, beauty, large-catalog or general store) before any design work.
steps: Go to Online Store > Themes and scroll to explore free themes. The source names Dawn (minimal, versatile — suits fashion, beauty and general stores), Horizon (modern, bold — for stronger visual impact) and Trade (built for larger catalogs with many products).
Always click the theme and choose view demo before installing. Preview first rather than installing blind.
If it matches your brand direction, click add to theme library, then publish; the storefront updates within seconds.

Weigh paid themes carefully: the source cites $200–$400 with extra built-in features, and argues most beginners do not need them because free themes now offer clean layouts, strong mobile optimization and fast loading. Speed matters because visitors abandon slow pages, especially on mobile.
Do not over-analyze: the source says you can switch themes later, so pick one matching your niche and catalog size and move on.
caveats: Theme names, features and paid pricing change; verify in the current theme store.
Theme choice is not a permanent decision — treat it as reversible.

cards.title: Turn a default theme into a brand with global settings and a transparent logo
cards.summary: The fast foundational pass — hero H1, colors, typography, logo — that makes a template feel intentional before deeper section work.
cards.use_when: Customizing a freshly published theme so it stops looking generic and starts reading as a real brand.
steps: Open Edit theme. The left panel lists sections; the right panel is a live preview you refresh as you change things.
Start with the header structure and alignment even if your logo is not ready yet.
Go to Theme settings > Colors: set the primary brand color and keep the background white. The source argues white backgrounds generally convert better because products stand out on them.

Go to typography settings and choose simple, readable fonts (the source names Montserrat and Source Sans Pro). Decorative fonts are explicitly called a clarity risk — if customers struggle to read, they leave.

Generate a minimal logo with an AI image tool or free logo tools; text-based logos work well. Then use a background remover such as remove.bg to export a transparent PNG — the source calls messy logo backgrounds a common beginner mistake that instantly lowers perceived quality.
Upload via the header/theme settings and adjust size so it looks balanced, not oversized or tiny.
Optionally build a cohesive palette by asking an AI for a primary, secondary and accent hex set, then paste the primary hex into the color field and keep contrast high so text stays legible.
Optionally use the theme editor's AI section recommendations: describe your brand in a few sentences and it generates layout suggestions for your niche.
caveats: AI-generated palettes and sections are starting points; you still apply and review them inside the theme editor.
White background and font choices are the source's conversion-oriented opinions, not tested rules for every brand.

cards.title: Structure header, menu style and announcement bar for product count
cards.summary: Match navigation pattern to catalog size and use a benefit-driven announcement bar to guide first actions.
cards.use_when: Configuring the storefront header, menus and announcement bar before driving traffic to the store.
steps: In the theme editor, click header and review layout options — logo left or centered, depending on the aesthetic you want.
Choose the menu style by catalog size: a drawer menu for stores with heavy mobile traffic, a dropdown menu for smaller catalogs, a mega menu for large stores with many categories.
Keep the menu short. The source's reasoning: too many items create confusion and confused buyers rarely complete purchases.
Enable the announcement bar and write a benefit-led prompt, e.g. free shipping on orders over $50 or a limited-time launch sale. The source frames these as small urgency cues that guide action.
Refresh the preview and check the header/announcement combination doesn't crowd the top of the page, then re-check in mobile view.
caveats: Menu-style suitability is the source's rule of thumb; test what fits your own traffic mix.
Urgency prompts should reflect real terms — do not advertise a threshold or sale you will not honor.

cards.title: Build a hero banner that communicates one clear benefit
cards.summary: Hero image, headline, subtext and CTA decisions with a mobile contrast check.
cards.use_when: Designing or refining the homepage hero section — the first thing visitors see from ads or social traffic.
steps: Source the image direction first: prompt an AI with something like "produce a hero banner image that matches this brand" to get a concept aligned to your niche and positioning.

Then use Shopify's built-in image library: click the hero section, select image, explore free images, and search niche keywords (fitness, skincare, jewelry). Choose high-resolution files only — a blurry banner immediately hurts credibility.
Set a headline that communicates a benefit or outcome rather than a product name; the source's example is "confidence starts with skin."

Add one short subtext sentence supporting the message, then a clear CTA button such as Shop now or Explore collection. The source says never leave a banner without a button because buttons drive the next click.
Set the main homepage hero heading to an H1 tag so search engines can read the page structure.
Preview on mobile: confirm the headline is readable and does not blend into the image. If contrast is weak, add a subtle overlay behind the text.
caveats: Free stock imagery can look generic; the source treats image direction and resolution as the quality levers, not the source.
H1 placement is a structural SEO practice the source asserts, not a ranking guarantee.

cards.title: Generate policies from Shopify templates and customize every detail
cards.summary: Use built-in policy templates, then edit shipping and refund specifics so disputes and chargebacks are reduced.
cards.use_when: Setting up privacy, terms, shipping and refund policies before the store accepts public orders.
steps: Go to Settings > Policies. Shopify provides templates for Privacy Policy, Terms of Service, Shipping Policy and Refund Policy; click create from template for each.
Read through each generated policy and confirm it matches your actual business rather than publishing the default text unchanged.

Draft shipping terms you will actually honor: delivery windows, handling time and conditions. The source notes that ignoring shipping details is a common beginner mistake that leads to disputes and unnecessary refunds.
For the refund policy, decide the return window in days and who pays return shipping. The source ties clarity here directly to fewer chargebacks.

If drafting is slow, prompt an AI (e.g. "write a simple shipping policy for this brand") for a starting draft, then replace every placeholder with your real terms — the source warns never to copy blindly.
Save and confirm Shopify places the policies in the footer automatically.
caveats: Templates are a starting point, not legal advice; the source repeatedly instructs reviewing and customizing them.
Policy content must reflect what you actually do, or the mismatch creates the disputes it was meant to prevent.

cards.title: Write a product page by describing the product, then generating and rewriting the copy
cards.summary: Replace supplier text with benefit-led descriptions using Shopify's AI writing assistant plus short paragraphs and a brand-voice edit.
cards.use_when: Adding a product to the catalog and building the PDP copy that will carry conversion.
steps: Go to Products > Add product. Write a simple, specific title so customers immediately know what the item is without guessing.
Avoid copying supplier descriptions — the source says generic supplier text lowers trust because it reads overused.
Write to benefits, not just features: explain how the product helps, improves or solves a problem, in short paragraphs that scan easily.
To move faster, click the sparkle icon in the description box, briefly describe the product and let Shopify generate a draft — then edit it to match your brand voice.
Keep formatting clean; better readability supports conversion.
Also enable Track quantity and enter your available stock so you cannot oversell. The source notes dropshippers may disable tracking, but says tracking helps prevent order issues.
Set the search engine listing preview: include your main keyword in the page title and write a concise meta description explaining what the product is.
caveats: AI drafts are editing starting points, not finished copy.
The track-quantity advice is framed with a legitimate dropshipping exception, so it is a situational default.

cards.title: Use compare-at pricing, variants and 1000px+ images on the product page
cards.summary: Pricing display, product options and image quality checks that shape perceived value and reduce refunds.
cards.use_when: Completing the pricing, options and imagery fields for each new product listing.
steps: Fill in both price and compare at price. The source's example: if the product sells for $49, set compare-at to $79 and Shopify displays the higher price struck through, creating perceived value. Keep the discount realistic — the source says overstated discounts reduce credibility.
If the product has options like size or color, click add options and create variants (for example small, medium, large). Clear options smooth the buying process.
Configure physical package dimensions in the product details so shipping calculations have accurate inputs.
Upload bright, clear photos at least 1000x1000 pixels. Zoom in and check for blur; replace anything low quality. Sharper images build confidence and the source links this to fewer refund requests.
Add product tags so the item can be grouped and found by your collections and internal search.
Order the images so the first shot reads as the clearest representation of the product.
caveats: Compare-at pricing only reads as credible when the original price is genuine; the source warns that exaggerated discounts backfire.
The 1000x1000 pixel figure is the source's minimum guidance, not a platform requirement.

cards.title: Choose manual vs. automatic collections and surface them on the homepage
cards.summary: Collection type decision by catalog growth, plus the homepage section that gets products out of the backend.
cards.use_when: Organizing the catalog into browsable categories and featuring them on the homepage.
steps: Go to Products > Collections > Create collection and name it clearly so customers know exactly what is inside.

Choose manual collections to hand-pick individual products; choose automatic (smart) collections to group products by rules. The source's reasoning: automatic collections save time as the store grows.
Add a collection image and a short description explaining what the category includes — this is what makes the browse step feel intentional rather than random.
Return to the homepage in the theme editor, add a section that features your collection and select the correct category from the section settings.
Preview the page and confirm products are now visible in the storefront rather than hidden in the backend.
Use product tags consistently at the product level if you rely on smart collections, since rule-based grouping depends on those fields.
caveats: Smart collection behavior depends on the rules and tags you configure; a mistagged product silently lands in the wrong collection.
Collection image and description quality is what the source credits for perceived structure, not the collection type itself.

cards.title: Prune and rebuild the main menu around collections, then test it on mobile
cards.summary: Navigation hygiene as a conversion issue: remove defaults, add collections, verify on a phone.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up store navigation before launch so customers can actually find products.
steps: Go to Online Store > Navigation and open your main menu. Remove default links such as home, catalog and contact that add no shopping path. The source's claim: cleaner menus convert better because they reduce decision fatigue.
Click add menu item, name it clearly, click link, choose collections, select the matching collection and save. Repeat for your main categories.
Limit the number of links — the source argues more options make customers hesitate.

Open the theme preview and switch to the mobile view. Review spacing, test dropdown behavior and check the menu does not feel crowded; most buyers shop on their phone, so the layout must be thumb-friendly.
Click every link, submenu and collection to confirm there are no broken paths or dead ends.
Confirm your policies and support pages are reachable from the footer.
caveats: Menu naming and link-picking flows change between Shopify versions; verify the current admin.
The 'fewer menu items convert better' position is the source's stated rationale, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Order the homepage: hero, collections, featured products, then trust blocks
cards.summary: Sequence homepage sections so the page reads as guided rather than random, adding testimonials and an FAQ.
cards.use_when: Arranging or auditing homepage sections after products and collections exist.
steps: Open the homepage in the theme editor and use Add section.
Add a testimonials section. Even a few short quotes raise credibility; the source says pre-launch feedback from friends or early testers is acceptable when you have no buyers yet.
Add an FAQ section covering the questions customers actually ask — shipping times, return policy, sizing. The source ties FAQs to reduced hesitation and fewer support emails.

Review the whole page top to bottom and check the order: hero, then collections, then featured products, then trust elements like testimonials and FAQs. When it flows in that order the homepage feels guided rather than random.
Look for anything that feels cluttered; the source compares the homepage to a storefront window where a random layout sends visitors away quickly.
Re-check the same sequence in mobile view.
caveats: Testimonials must be genuine; the source allows early tester feedback but misrepresenting reviews undermines the trust the section exists to build.
Section names and availability vary by theme.

cards.title: Activate Shopify Payments plus at least one alternative gateway
cards.summary: Payment setup that connects payouts and adds a familiar fallback option for hesitant and international buyers.
cards.use_when: Enabling payment methods before taking the store off password protection.
steps: In admin, find Shopify Payments, click choose a provider, select it and complete setup — this connects payouts directly to your bank account and enables major card brands without separate integrations.
Add at least one alternative method. The source calls activating only one method a common beginner mistake because it limits flexibility and can reduce trust.
Enable PayPal: it is often already linked to your account email; otherwise click activate PayPal, log in and grant permissions — the source estimates about a minute.
Consider that PayPal is familiar to international customers and may increase their comfort at checkout.
Check what gateways are actually available in your region; the source notes some countries require specific providers.
Reason from the source's principle: the smoother the checkout path, the less friction stands between a ready buyer and a completed order.
caveats: Gateway availability and setup flows vary by country and change over time — verify what your region supports.
Identity or document verification may be required and can delay payouts.

cards.title: Define shipping zones, rates and a free-shipping threshold
cards.summary: Zone, rate-model and threshold decisions that keep delivery expectations clear and lift average order value.
cards.use_when: Configuring shipping and delivery settings before launch, including whether to ship internationally.
steps: Go to Settings > Shipping and delivery, open your primary zone and define the countries you actually ship to. Decide deliberately between domestic-only and worldwide — the source notes global shipping adds complexity and starting simple is usually better.

Pick a pricing model. Flat rate means a single fixed charge customers understand; dynamic rates calculate in real time by weight and carrier. The source says flat rate is often easier for beginners to manage and avoids confusion.
Consider a free shipping threshold — the source's example is free over $75 — because customers respond strongly to free shipping and will add items to qualify, which lifts average order value.
If you ship internationally, create separate zones and set higher flat rates or calculated rates for them.
Add a handling buffer where it applies; the source describes adding around $5 to cover handling.
State delivery times clearly everywhere shipping is mentioned. The source links long shipping without clear expectations to complaints.
caveats: The $75 threshold and $5 handling buffer are the source's illustrative examples, not benchmarks for your margins — model them against your own cost structure.
Carrier-calculated rates depend on accurate product weights and package dimensions.

cards.title: Configure taxes by verifying your own obligations first
cards.summary: Use Shopify's automatic tax tools, but establish nexus or VAT registration requirements before relying on them.
cards.use_when: Setting up tax collection for a store selling domestically or across borders.
steps: Go to Settings > Taxes and duties. The source's starting point: requirements depend entirely on your location, so verify your obligations under local law rather than guessing.
Enable automatic tax collection, which calculates based on the customer's location, and review the rates configured for your region to confirm they align.
If registered in the United States, review your state nexus rules to determine whether you must collect sales tax.
If operating in the European Union, check VAT requirements and registration thresholds.
Consult a tax professional if obligations are unclear — the source says mistakes here become expensive quickly.
Once configured correctly, Shopify handles the calculations in the background.
caveats: The source explicitly defers to local law and professionals; do not treat Shopify's defaults as compliance.
Nexus and VAT rules change; re-verify as you add markets.

cards.title: Install three apps, not ten — reviews, email, tracking
cards.summary: A lean app stack with a review tool chosen for free-plan strength versus photo-centric reviews.
cards.use_when: Adding apps to a new store without degrading page speed before launch.
steps: Go to Apps, open the Shopify app store and search only for essential tools. The source says most new stores need three things: a review app, an email app and a tracking/analytics app.

Prioritize the review app because the source says reviews increase conversions almost immediately. Two named options are Judge.me and Loox: Judge.me is described as stronger on its free plan, Loox as focused on photo-based reviews.
Enable automatic review requests so customers receive follow-up emails after purchase.
Install a tracking/analytics app so you can see traffic sources, best-performing products and where people drop off. The source's framing: guessing is not a strategy.
Resist installing many apps at once — the source says every added app adds weight and site speed affects conversion. Start lean and expand only when the business needs more.
Review pricing and features before installing each app, especially as a store scales past the free tier.
caveats: App features and free-tier limits change; the source's app comparisons reflect its recording time.
Review apps may require configuration to avoid sending requests that look spammy or mistimed.

cards.title: Run the pre-launch checklist: store details, domain, test order, mobile, policies, links
cards.summary: The final verification pass that catches small errors before the store goes public.
cards.use_when: The last step before removing password protection and making the store publicly accessible.
steps: Verify store details: Settings > Store details — business name correct, email accurate, and store currency matching your target market. The source warns the wrong currency can confuse buyers and cause checkout abandonment.
Check the domain: Settings > Domains should show Connected. If it still shows pending, allow a few hours for DNS propagation rather than launching on a broken domain.

Test payments: enable test mode in payment settings, place a test order yourself, walk through the full checkout and confirm the order confirmation email actually arrives. Then disable test mode before launch.
Review the store on your phone: scroll slowly, tap every button, add a product to the cart and complete checkout. Most customers shop on mobile, so the experience must feel smooth.
Open every policy page from the footer and read the first paragraph — confirm your business name appears correctly and no placeholder or incomplete text remains.
Click every menu item, submenu and collection to confirm no link leads to an empty or broken page.
caveats: The source frames these as low-effort checks that prevent large post-launch problems; skipping the payment test is called out as risky because failed payments damage trust quickly.
Test mode must be turned back off — launching with it active blocks real orders.

cards.title: Remove password protection and verify the live store as a customer
cards.summary: The publishing step plus a first-visitor walkthrough of the live domain.
cards.use_when: Taking the store public for the first time, immediately before sharing the link on social or with testers.
steps: Go to Online Store and click remove password. The source describes this as the single step that makes the store publicly accessible — no preview mode, no restriction.
Confirm the correct theme is live: go to Online Store > Themes and check your current theme shows as live. If it does not, click publish and confirm.
Open a new browser tab, manually type your domain, and browse as a first-time visitor would: homepage, open a product, add it to cart, walk through checkout.
Then start distributing the link — social bios, messages, a friend — and collect feedback rather than continuing to polish.
The source's closing framing: the goal is progress, not perfection; keep improving and testing after launch.
Also enable the email and SMS marketing opt-in checkboxes at the checkout/sign-in step so buyer consent is captured directly.
caveats: Launching before collecting feedback is preferable to endless pre-launch tweaking, per the source; but re-run the checklist if any admin changes were made after the test order.
Marketing opt-ins must match the consent rules in your jurisdiction.

Checkout Marketing Opt-Ins: Enabling both email and SMS checkboxes at the checkout/sign-in page to capture direct marketing consent from buyers.

Password Removal (Launch): Navigating to Online Store > Preferences to disable the password protection toggle and push the store live to the public.

Skip. Promotional pitches for the Shopify $1 trial or generic motivational statements about starting a business.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard Shopify backend configuration). Volume. ~350 words.
